doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Breaking the color line in the fraternity system with Don Thomas
summary: Collier and housemates pushed ELS to accept Don Thomas, the first black member of a fraternity there; blackballing is then explained.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: No, this would have been later, after I was maybe a junior or something, ‘48, somewhere around in there. But during that time I and three or four or five or six other members of my house, because there were no blacks in any fraternity and hardly any blacks on the campus mind you, but there were no blacks in any fraternity. And we said, this group of us said, we’re going to do something about this. And so there was a young freshman called Don Thomas and last I heard he was living in New York on the Upper West Side, and Don was a big, good looking guy, had come from Oberlin. His father had been I think the postmaster in Oberlin, and had grown up in a circumstance where blacks were pretty well accepted because Oberlin was one of the first colleges in the United States to take blacks, and so it was a whole different situation he had grown up in. And I guess his dad wanted him to go to some other place so that he’d get a little taste what the real world was like. But he was a big, good looking guy, he was athletic, he went out for basketball, he was a happy-go-lucky guy, he liked to drink beer, he was a party boy. He was a classic fraternity guy. Absolutely the guy, had he been white, all of the fraternities would have been giving him bids. But they didn’t. And so finally I said look — or here’s — one of us — I don’t want to take all the credit for all of this. I said we’ve got to, this guy is a guy who you can’t think of any reason for turning him down. You can’t say he’s too short, you can’t say he’s a nerd, you can’t say anything about him. And so we put him up, and we fought. And it took us a couple of months to fight that through the fraternity. Fortunately in ELS we didn’t have a black ball system. You had a majority vote. So if the majority wanted him, and it took us a struggle to get the majority, but we did get that majority, and so we broke the color line in the fraternity system there at Hamilton. And once he was in the house it was a done deal. Nobody cared. The party guys in the house, they immediately took to him. They were all out running around drinking beer and not doing their homework. I was Don’s upper class advisor so I was always sticking it to him saying come on, you put your tail down in that chair and let’s see — I want to see these grades. But the unhappy result was that all of the other houses breathed a sigh of relief © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

saying ELS is going to take care of the blacks, and so we had a moral crisis over every black kid that was admitted to Hamilton after that. But I think it helped the administration to see that the students were not going to have a problem with this, they just weren’t. And so then of course things began to change and the situation began to open up and obviously improve. But I wanted that on record.
That was what you had at Hamilton in those days. And it was obviously time to change.
You mentioned you didn’t have a black ball system. How do you black ball somebody?

Well a blackball goes back to the old business of joining a club I think in London where you had the white balls and a blackball and if you favored the admission you threw the white ball in so it was all secret. But if you threw a blackball in and if there were a blackball in the bowl then it was no.
So one person could block it.

That’s right. I think in practice it didn’t quite work that way because at the beginning of the year the houses were competing with each other to get the people they considered to be the most desirable. So you had a committee. And the committee generally was empowered to make decisions. But later in the year if you were going to take in additional people, maybe you were going to take in a sophomore for example, who suddenly everybody liked or thought why isn’t he in this or whatever, somebody was promoting. But then you would have a voting system.
So originally the committee, the committee had to be able to act rapidly because some other house is going to grab this guy so, you know, so you would.
